name: Napping / NSDR / yoga nidra
lead: Napping, non-sleep deep rest (NSDR) and yoga nidra are short rest practices used to recover energy, reduce stress and make up for lost sleep. A nap is a short daytime sleep; yoga nidra is a guided, lying-down meditation often described as a state between waking and sleeping; NSDR is a newer label for similar guided-rest protocols.[1][2] In looksmaxxing communities they are used as part of a recovery routine meant to support how a person looks: more rested eyes and skin, better training recovery and more alertness and energy.[7][13]

The appearance link has a research anchor. In a 2013 Karolinska Institutet experiment, 40 observers rated photographs of 10 people taken after normal sleep and after 31 hours of sleep deprivation; the sleep-deprived faces were rated as having more hanging eyelids, redder and more swollen eyes, darker under-eye circles, paler skin, more wrinkles or fine lines and droopier mouth corners.[17] Napping and rest practices are used by people trying to avoid that tired look.

Forum authors describe naps as an overlooked recovery tool, arguing that short midday sleep supports alertness, memory and training recovery, and some tie rest to aesthetics through a fresher, less tired appearance.[7] Athletic-performance research gives a related picture: a 2021 narrative review examined how daytime napping affects athletic performance.[8]

Research on naps reports benefits for alertness and memory, and early trials of yoga nidra report effects on sleep, stress and mood in small groups.[1][2][9][10] Napping is also a long-standing cultural habit, from the Mediterranean siesta to the Chinese wushui.[14]

chain: Short nap or guided rest between waking hours
Less sleep debt and lower stress
More energy and training recovery, fresher-looking face
angle.text: People use naps and guided rest to offset short nights and support training and daily energy. Practitioners link better-rested days with a fresher look and better workout recovery.

paras: Naps are categorised by duration, such as micro naps of a few minutes, power naps of 10-30 minutes and full-cycle naps of about 90 minutes.[1] Wikipedia reports that early afternoon is when sleepiness typically peaks and describes 20-30 minutes as a common recommendation for adults.[1] A NASA study is reported to show a 26-minute nap improved alertness by 54% and performance by 34% in pilots.[1]

Sleep inertia, the grogginess after waking, is more likely after longer naps that reach slow-wave sleep and rarely lasts beyond 30 minutes in people who are not sleep-deprived.[1] A 2016 meta-analysis linked habitual naps over an hour with higher cardiovascular and metabolic risk, with no causal link established, while naps up to 40 minutes showed no such association.[1] Sleep in general aids memory consolidation.[3]

Wikipedia lists nap types by purpose: power, recovery, prophylactic (before an expected sleep loss), safety (for pilots and drivers), appetitive (for enjoyment), habitual, caffeine and essential naps. Sleepiness typically peaks in mid-afternoon, which is why early afternoon is described as the usual time to nap, and adults are usually advised to keep naps to 20 to 30 minutes.[1] Short habitual naps after study are described as most helpful for memory, and prescribed napping is used to reduce excessive daytime sleepiness in narcolepsy.[1]

sections.h: Sleep inertia and the caffeine nap
paras: Sleep inertia is the impaired thinking and clumsiness that follow waking; in most cases it lasts 15 to 30 minutes. Waking from slow-wave sleep produces more of it than waking from lighter sleep, and sleep deprivation makes it more likely, which is why short naps under about 30 minutes are used to avoid deep sleep.[15] Caffeine blocks adenosine receptors, and caffeine taken before a short nap is described as possibly reducing inertia, though tolerance affects how well this works; other countermeasures studied include dawn-like light, melodic alarms, temperature changes and exercise.[15]

The word siesta comes from the Latin hora sexta, the sixth hour around noon, and the custom began in Roman times around the Mediterranean; Cicero and Suetonius mention it, and Einhard describes Charlemagne's summer naps of two or three hours.[14] Midday napping is common in South America and in China, where surveys suggest about two-thirds of people nap for about 30 minutes, while a 2009 survey reported 16.2 percent of Spaniards napping daily.[14] A Greek study in 2007 associated siestas with a 37 percent reduction in coronary mortality, though later studies reached conflicting conclusions, possibly because of confounders such as physical activity.[14]

Cornell psychologist James Maas coined the term power nap, which revived interest in midday rest in the US and UK, and sleep researcher Charles Czeisler has called mid-afternoon a great time for a nap.[14]

Yoga nidra's modern form draws on Western relaxation methods; Satyananda Saraswati popularised a structured method in 1976, and Richard Miller developed iRest for soldiers with PTSD.[2] Claimed benefits include reduced anxiety and better sleep; a small trial of 45 male athletes found improved sleep latency and efficiency versus progressive muscle relaxation.[2]
NSDR is a newer name for similar guided-rest protocols and is not covered in Wikipedia's yoga nidra article.[2]

The word yoga nidra appears in the Mahabharata and the Devimahatmya as a state or a goddess rather than a technique, and Hatha and Raja yoga texts from the 11th and 12th centuries use it as a synonym for samadhi. Wikipedia reports that the modern guided method derives mainly from 19th and 20th century Western relaxation methods, including Annie Payson Call's Power through Repose (1891) and Edmund Jacobson's You Must Relax! (1934), and that Dennis Boyes used the term in a 1973 French book.[2]

Satyananda Saraswati's eight stages are internalisation, resolve (sankalpa), rotation of consciousness, breath awareness, manifestation of opposites, creative visualisation, repeated resolve and externalisation. Scholars Jason Birch and Jacqueline Hargreaves found the multi-stage technique absent from ancient texts, and Swami Rama taught a broader variant based on a body-point practice in shavasana.[2] Richard Miller's iRest was developed with Walter Reed Army Medical Center and the Department of Defense for veterans with PTSD; the US Army Surgeon General endorsed yoga nidra for chronic pain in 2010.[2] In 2021 Uma Dinsmore-Tuli and Nirlipta Tuli published a declaration arguing yoga nidra had been commodified, naming several founders.[2]

Research listed on Wikipedia includes a small four-week trial of 45 male athletes (2022), a randomised trial in insomnia patients (2021), a heart-rate-variability study (2012), a pilot in hypertensive subjects (2021), a study in university students on life stress and self-esteem (2019) and a functional-connectivity study of meditators and novices (2024); the article notes many trials are small.[2]

Polyphasic sleep means sleeping in more than two periods a day, and schedules such as Everyman (about 3 hours at night plus three 20-minute naps), Uberman (30 minutes every four hours) and Buckminster Fuller's Dymaxion (30 minutes every six hours) circulate online. Wikipedia reports a 1989 study of 99 solo sailors by Claudio Stampi concluding that polyphasic strategies helped sustained performance, and that a 2021 National Sleep Foundation consensus report described adverse impacts of polyphasic patterns.[16] A Hacker News thread discusses it as napping taken to the extreme.[11]

One looksmax.org thread presents the power nap as a forgotten part of recovery, describing short naps as improving reaction time, attention and memory consolidation, and warning that long naps can leave users groggy.[7] Replies in the thread mention sleeping for hours when attempting a nap and using phone alarms to limit it.[7] A separate thread discusses social perceptions of men napping.[12]

Nap research includes the NASA pilot study and the 2016 meta-analysis.[1] A 2021 narrative review examined daytime napping and athletic performance.[8] A Zurich crossover study in 70 healthy women found that a hypnotic suggestion to sleep deeper, played before a 90-minute nap, increased slow-wave sleep by 81 percent.[4]

Yoga nidra trials include a randomized sleep-lab feasibility study in 22 adults with self-reported insomnia,[5] a randomized trial in chronic insomnia,[6] and trials on stress and self-esteem in university students[9] and on anxiety and insomnia in COVID-19 frontline health workers.[10] No studies were found on NSDR as a named protocol.

A 2013 laboratory experiment at Karolinska Institutet, published in Sleep, examined how sleep deprivation changes facial appearance and found observers rated sleep-deprived faces as more tired-looking; it did not measure naps directly.[17]

lore.intro: On looksmax.org naps and rest appear within sleep-and-recovery discussions as a way to support performance and appearance.[7]

claims.claim: Power naps improve recovery, performance and aesthetics
claims.believers: A looksmax.org author says mid-day naps improve reaction time, attention, decision-making and memory and describes recovery and aesthetic benefits.[7]
claims.experts: Wikipedia reports benefits for alertness and memory from naps, and a narrative review examined naps and athletic performance; no studies were found on naps and facial appearance.[1][8]

claims.believers: The same author reports napping for too long left him feeling worse.[7]
claims.experts: Wikipedia describes sleep inertia as more likely after longer naps and reports a 2016 meta-analysis associating habitual naps over an hour with higher risk markers, without establishing causation.[1]

claims.claim: Guided rest such as yoga nidra improves sleep and lowers stress
claims.believers: Practitioners describe yoga nidra as deeply relaxing and sleep-supporting.[2]
claims.experts: Small randomized trials report effects on insomnia and stress outcomes.[5][6][9]

claims.claim: Sleep loss shows on the face and rest reverses it
claims.believers: Users link rest to a fresher look, less puffiness and brighter eyes.[7]
claims.experts: A 2013 experiment found faces photographed after 31 hours of sleep deprivation were rated as having darker circles, swollen eyes and paler skin; no study tested whether naps reverse this.[17]

claims.claim: Polyphasic schedules can replace a full night's sleep
claims.believers: Online communities discuss Everyman and Uberman-style schedules as time-efficient sleep.[11]
claims.experts: Wikipedia reports a 2021 National Sleep Foundation consensus report on adverse effects of polyphasic sleep and says no scientific evidence shows productivity benefits.[16]

claims.claim: A coffee before a nap boosts alertness
claims.believers: Fans of the caffeine nap say the drink kicks in as they wake.[15]
claims.experts: Wikipedia reports that caffeine taken before a short nap may reduce sleep inertia, with tolerance affecting results.[15]

card.summary: Short naps and guided deep-rest sessions for recovery; naps have decent evidence, yoga nidra is promising but small.
card.note: Long habitual naps associated with health risks in observational data.

quick.overview:
These are brief rest practices: daytime naps, and guided relaxation known as yoga nidra or NSDR.

Naps show benefits for alertness and learning, while yoga nidra research is small.
quick.mechanism: Naps restore alertness through short sleep; yoga nidra uses guided body awareness to produce deep relaxation.
quick.risks: Long naps can cause grogginess, and habitual long napping is linked observationally with health risks.
